topics.title: Network Layer Fundamentals
topics.description: The network layer is responsible for delivering packets from the source host to the destination host across multiple networks. It performs logical addressing, routing, forwarding and packet handling to ensure that data reaches the correct destination.

subtopics.title: Purpose of the Network Layer
subtopics.theory: The network layer is the third layer in the OSI model and is responsible for host-to-host communication across different networks. While the data link layer manages communication between devices on the same network, the network layer handles communication across multiple interconnected networks. Its main goal is to ensure that packets generated by a source device reach the correct destination device regardless of the number of intermediate routers involved.

subtopics.title: Key Responsibilities of the Network Layer
subtopics.theory: The network layer performs several critical tasks including logical addressing, packet routing, packet forwarding and packet fragmentation. Logical addressing allows devices to be uniquely identified using IP addresses. Routing determines the best path for packets to travel across networks. Forwarding moves packets from one router interface to another. Fragmentation divides large packets into smaller pieces so they can pass through networks with smaller maximum transmission units.

subtopics.title: What is Packetizing
subtopics.theory: Packetizing is the process of encapsulating data received from the transport layer into packets before sending them to the data link layer. Each packet contains both the data payload and a header containing information such as source IP address, destination IP address, and control fields. Packetizing allows large data streams to be broken into manageable pieces for efficient transmission across networks.

subtopics.title: Encapsulation at the Network Layer
subtopics.theory: During encapsulation the network layer adds its header to the data received from the transport layer. This header contains important information used for routing and delivery. The packet is then passed to the data link layer which further encapsulates it into a frame before transmission over the physical medium.

subtopics.title: What is Routing
subtopics.theory: Routing is the process of selecting the best path for data packets to travel from a source network to a destination network. Routers use routing algorithms and routing tables to determine the optimal route based on factors such as distance, network congestion and link cost.

subtopics.title: Routing Tables
subtopics.theory: Routers maintain routing tables that contain information about available networks and the best paths to reach them. Each entry in a routing table typically includes the destination network, next hop address, outgoing interface and path cost. When a router receives a packet it examines the destination IP address and consults its routing table to determine where to forward the packet.

subtopics.title: What is Packet Forwarding
subtopics.theory: Forwarding is the process of transferring a packet from one router interface to another based on the information in the routing table. Once a router determines the best path for a packet it forwards the packet to the next hop device along that path.

subtopics.title: Forwarding Decision Process
subtopics.theory: When a router receives a packet it reads the destination IP address from the packet header. It then compares this address with entries in its routing table to determine the next hop. The router forwards the packet through the appropriate interface so it can continue traveling toward its final destination.

subtopics.title: Why Fragmentation is Needed
subtopics.theory: Different networks support different maximum transmission unit (MTU) sizes which define the maximum packet size that can be transmitted. If a packet is larger than the MTU of the next network it must be divided into smaller fragments so that it can pass through the network successfully.

subtopics.title: Fragmentation and Reassembly
subtopics.theory: When fragmentation occurs the original packet is split into multiple smaller fragments each containing its own header information. These fragments travel independently through the network and are reassembled at the destination device to reconstruct the original packet.

subtopics.title: IP Addressing
subtopics.theory: Logical addressing allows each device in a network to be uniquely identified using an Internet Protocol address. Unlike MAC addresses which are hardware-based and used locally, IP addresses allow devices to communicate across multiple networks. IPv4 addresses are 32-bit identifiers typically written in dotted decimal format such as 192.168.1.1.

subtopics.title: Importance of Logical Addressing
subtopics.theory: Logical addressing allows routers to determine where packets should be delivered. Without logical addresses it would be impossible to route packets across global networks such as the Internet. Logical addressing is therefore essential for large-scale communication systems.
